This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust has lost a longtime institutional investor in Tesla Inc. (TSLA, Financials) , saying it sold its remaining shares in April to conclude a stake it initially formed in 2013.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with TSLA.

Is TSLA fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

TSLA GF Value chart

The Baillie Gifford (Trades, Portfolio)-managed fund invested nearly $470 million into Tesla over 13 years, making almost $6.2 billion in realized profit. The investment yielded 13 times the invested funds.

Scottish Mortgage said most of Tesla's promise in autonomous driving and robotics was already factored into its value. Increased rivalry in the electric car space, especially in China, was also mentioned by the fund. The trust has also cut its exposure to SpaceX.

SpaceX made up 11.1% of the fund's assets as of Wednesday, down from 15% as of Sept. 30. Scottish Mortgage initially bought into SpaceX in December 2018, investing about $200 million through 2021.

The position contributed 8 percentage points to the trust's 31.5% net asset value return for the six months to Sept. 30. The fund said the decision to cut the investment reflected portfolio discipline and not a lack of faith in SpaceX.

The selling of shares has helped reduce borrowing . What to watch next: Will Scottish Mortgage continue to slash SpaceX as it reshapes its portfolio after the company's public debut?

Elon Musk says SpaceX (SPCX) will likely top $500 billion in ARR by December 2027, roughly triple the $180 billion analyst consensus.

SpaceX's third quarter annualizes to $58 billion, so Musk's target demands about 8.6 times that level in roughly 14 months.

Rocket Lab (RKLB) and AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) carry market caps of $31 billion and $10 billion, dwarfed by SpaceX's $1.76 trillion valuation.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Elon Musk just put a number on SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) that sits above every revenue model on Wall Street. He spoke at the Baron Investment Conference, and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) and SpaceX watcher Sawyer Merritt relayed the remark on X:

24/7 Wall St.

"It seems quite likely that our ARR in Dec 2027 will exceed $500B. This is not a promise, this is my best guess. $1 trillion..."

Merritt's summary added that $1 trillion is "not out of the question" and said Musk had "reiterated" the view.

Musk's Floor Clears Even the Most Bullish Analyst

Thirty-seven analysts put average fiscal 2027 revenue at roughly $180 billion. The high estimate is $290 billion and the low is about $72 billion. Musk's floor comes to about 2.8 times consensus and sits roughly $210 billion above the Street's most aggressive model.

ARR, or annual recurring revenue, usually takes one month of recurring sales and multiplies it by 12. Analysts model total revenue for the full year. A company that reaches a $500 billion run rate in December would book much less than that across the whole year, so the two figures don't line up exactly. Musk did not define the term, and he presented the figure as his best guess.

That quarter annualizes to $58.4 billion, and Musk's target is about 8.6 times that level, roughly 14 months out.

Key Takeaways

NIO stock rose 6% today with no company news, as XPeng, Tesla and Li Auto bounced with growth stocks after the post-midterm sell-off.

NIO's October deliveries fell 15.2% from a year earlier and XPeng's hit a record, but both stocks rose.

Analysts expect NIO's revenue to keep climbing, yet its forward price-to-sales multiple sits at a five-year low.

NIO's late-November report has to show margin and cash flow holding up for the rally to last.

NIO (NIO:NYSE) stock rose 6% today with no news from the company. It rode a bounce in growth stocks after two days of selling that followed Tuesday's midterm elections.

XPeng (XPEV:NYSE) rose 7% and Li Auto (LI:NASDAQ) rose 5%, neither with news of its own, while Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) gained 5%.

The whole group got the same bid

NIO and XPeng moved together even though their October numbers went opposite ways. NIO's deliveries fell 15.2% from a year earlier to 34,246. XPeng delivered a record 50,237, up 20%. Li Auto rose too, though analysts expect its revenue to grow just 0.5% in fiscal 2026. Investors were buying China's EV makers as a group.

Tesla had news: Elon Musk posted on X that it will wind down Cybertruck production around the middle of next year "to make room for increased Cybercab production." But at 189x forward earnings as of Thursday's close, Tesla trades on Cybercab, Robotaxi and Optimus far more than on one pickup.

Lucid Group (LCID:NASDAQ) rose 7% with no news either. Its question is still cash: $3 billion of total liquidity at June 30, which management then expected to last well into 2027.

NIO's own numbers have to follow

Analysts still expect NIO's revenue to climb from RMB87.5 billion in 2025 to RMB128 billion this year and RMB169 billion by 2028.

NIO (NIO): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Getting there takes volume NIO isn't delivering yet: its goal of more than 40,000 cars a month this quarter now needs November and December to average about 42,900. When it reports in late November, its vehicle margin has to hold near the second quarter's 18.5%, and operating cash flow has to stay positive, as management expects.

title: Tesla's Cybertruck is a masterclass in failing upwards

Tesla's Cybertruck is a masterclass in failing upwards

Getting things wrong is an essential part of getting things right. So for all of the ridicule and vandalism that Tesla's Cybertruck attracted during its brief life, it's hard to fault Elon Musk for trying new things. Especially since his investors seem to prize his successes while ignoring his failures.

Musk told followers on X that he is "winding down" production of the Cybertruck at his Texas gigafactory, and pivoting to production of his self-driving taxi, the Cybercab. The distinctively angular vehicle — which Musk variously claimed could serve as a boat and might one day traverse the surface of Mars — had been plagued with product recalls and negative brand associations. He had predicted annual sales of 250,000; in the first nine months of this year, Cox Automotive counts fewer than 12,000.

Trial and error is the raison d'être of tech companies, of course. Investors usually just ignore moonshots until they seem to have real value. Alphabet's "other bets" segment has made cumulative losses of around $57bn since 2014. But from that money pit sprang innovations like self-driving car company Waymo, which is now worth $147bn, according to PitchBook. And since the internet search giant has made $800bn of overall operating profit, nobody much minds.

Even Tesla bulls attributed little value to the Cybertruck. Former Tesla analyst Adam Jonas of Morgan Stanley, a reliable cheerleader, suggested in 2023 that it might be best thought of as a "cult car" rather than a blockbuster. Deutsche Bank, which has continually rated Tesla a "buy", sketched out numbers in 2024 that suggested the truck might contribute just 5 per cent of the company's gross profit by 2028.

Musk has moved on to the next big thing. Optimus, his humanoid robot, could be a "$25tn market cap situation", he has suggested, making Cybertruck feel like a blip. And flops can still add posthumous value to future projects. Electrical, mechanical and battery technology finessed to serve the ill-fated pick-up truck will help power Optimus and the Cybercab too.

If only the Cybertruck had proved as robust as the Elon Musk hype premium. Tesla's enterprise value equates to 11 times the coming year's forecast revenue, according to LSEG, where automakers General Motors and Ford trade at a fraction of a year's sales. Corporate sibling SpaceX, even at a depleted $1.7tn, also trades at an exuberant 11 times revenue. Musk wasn't so hot when it came to selling a pick-up truck, but he still knows how to sell himself.
